tool.name: LSRIOnDEM
tool.summary: Computes the Land Surface Ruggedness Index (LSRI), or Beasom's Ruggedness Index, directly from a DEM: contours are generated on the fly (the same Contour interval / Base contour / Z factor logic as Esri's own Contour tool, unsmoothed), then the total length of contour line within a circular neighborhood of each cell is reported (Beasom, Wiggers, and Giardino 1983). Higher values mean more, or more convoluted, contour line nearby, i.e. more rugged terrain.
tool.usage:
Beasom, Wiggers, and Giardino (1983) found that land surface ruggedness is closely related to the total length of contour lines crossing a fixed-size sample area -- a rugged, broken landscape needs many, tightly-spaced, winding contour lines to represent it, while a smooth or gently-rolling landscape needs few, widely-spaced, nearly-straight ones. They measured that total length directly with a tracing wheel over a 40-hectare circular sample area for a validation subset, but for routine use on many areas proposed a faster manual proxy instead: a dot-grid transparency laid over a printed topographic map, counting how many dots fell on a contour line (their "Land Surface Ruggedness Index"). That dot-counting shortcut only made sense because manually tracing every contour line by hand was tedious -- it does not apply here. This tool automates the more accurate of Beasom et al.'s two methods, the direct length measurement, over a moving circular neighborhood instead of a single fixed sample area, so you get a continuous ruggedness surface rather than one value per plot, with no need for the dot-grid estimate.
Contours are generated from the input DEM on the fly, using the same Contour interval, Base contour, and Z factor logic as Esri's own Contour tool (see those parameters below) -- unsmoothed, exactly like Esri's Contour tool, which has no smoothing option either. This matters here: smoothing would artificially shorten the very contour-line convolutedness this index is meant to measure, understating true ruggedness. The derived contours can optionally be saved as a feature class if you want to inspect or reuse them (for example, with the companion LSRI on Contours tool, which computes the same index directly from an existing contour feature class).
This tool is similar in spirit to Esri's Line Density tool, which also measures linear features within a circular neighborhood of each cell -- but Line Density reports a density (length per unit area), while this tool reports the total length directly, matching Beasom et al.'s original ruggedness concept. The two are not computed from each other; this tool measures contour length independently, using its own exact (non-rasterized) calculation.
This tool works on both projected and geographic (latitude/longitude) DEMs. On a geographic DEM, the neighborhood radius and the contour length it measures are computed as true ground (geodesic) distances, on the DEM's reference spheroid -- not a raw, misleading degree-space distance -- so results are correct at any latitude, including near the poles. The only approximation is the Cells radius unit, which uses a single representative ground cell size (at the DEM's central row) rather than one that varies by row; Meters, Kilometers, Feet, and Miles radius units need no such approximation.

dialogReference.para: The elevation raster (DEM) to contour and compute LSRI from. It must be single band. Both projected and geographic (latitude/longitude) coordinate systems are supported.
The output LSRI raster (floating point): the total length of contour line within the neighborhood radius of each cell, in the chosen length units. A suggested name is filled in from the input.

The interval, or distance, between contour lines. This can be any positive number, expressed in the DEM's own elevation (z) units -- or, if a Z factor other than 1 is set below, in whatever units that z-factor converts the elevation values to. A smaller interval creates more contour lines and so, all else equal, a higher LSRI; compare runs at the same interval.

The base contour value. Contours are generated above and below this value as needed to cover the entire value range of the input raster. The default is zero. For example, to create contours every 15 meters starting at 10 meters, use 10 for the base contour and 15 for the contour interval; the values contoured are 10, 25, 40, 55, and so on. Specifying a base contour does not prevent contours from being created above or below that value.

The unit conversion factor used when generating contours. The default value is 1. The contour lines are generated based on the z-values in the input raster, which are often measured in units of meters or feet. With the default value of 1, the contours will be in the same units as the z-values of the input raster. To create contours in a unit other than that of the z-values, set an appropriate value for the z-factor. It is not necessary to have the ground x,y and surface z-units be consistent for this tool.

How far the neighborhood extends around each cell, in the radius units below. There is no default -- choose a radius appropriate to the landscape scale and research question you're examining. (Beasom et al. picked their original 40-hectare, about 356.8-meter-radius sample plots mainly because that was a practical size to trace by hand on a printed 7.5-minute topographic map -- a paper-map constraint that doesn't apply to a computed neighborhood, so this tool does not impose that scale on you.) Larger values examine ruggedness at a coarser landscape scale.
The units of the radius. Cells applies the same radius everywhere, sized from the DEM's own cell size. Meters, Kilometers, Feet, and Miles are converted to the DEM's map units.
The linear units the output LSRI values are reported in (total contour length within the neighborhood). Default is Meters.

param.name: out_cell_size
param.displayname: Output cell size (default: same as input DEM)

dialogReference.para: The cell size of the output LSRI raster, in the DEM's own map units. Leave blank to match the input DEM's own cell size (the previous, and still default, behavior).

Contours are always traced at the DEM's full native resolution regardless of this setting, so accuracy is unaffected -- only the grid of cells the neighborhood length is reported on changes. Setting this coarser than the DEM is the most effective way to cut run time on a large, fine-resolution DEM (for example a 3+ million cell DEM with a fine contour interval over a large elevation range): the number of output cells, not the contour tracing itself, is what run time scales with.

Check this to save the contour polylines generated on the fly (unsmoothed, following the raster cell grid exactly) to the output feature class below, for example to inspect them or to reuse them with the companion LSRI on Contours tool.
The feature class to save the derived contour polylines to. Only used when "Save the contour feature class" is checked.

scriptExample.title: LSRI on DEM example (stand-alone script)
scriptExample.para: LSRI using a 500-meter neighborhood radius and a 10-meter contour interval, saving the derived contours.
scriptExample.code: import arcpy arcpy.ImportToolbox(r"C:\path\to\JennessEnterprisesTools.pyt") # your installed path is shown in this tool's run messages arcpy.jenness.LSRIOnDEM( in_raster=r"C:\Project\Elev.gdb\DEM", out_raster=r"C:\Project\Elev.gdb\DEM_LSRI", contour_interval=10, base_contour=0, z_factor=1, radius=500, radius_units="Meters", length_units="Meters", save_contours=True, out_contours=r"C:\Project\Elev.gdb\DEM_Contours")

dataIdInfo.idPurp: Land Surface Ruggedness Index (LSRI), or Beasom's Ruggedness Index, computed directly from a DEM: contours generated on the fly, then total contour length within a circular neighborhood of each cell (Beasom, Wiggers, and Giardino 1983).
dataIdInfo.idAbs: Generates unsmoothed contour polylines from a single-band DEM (matching Esri's own Contour tool's interval / base / z-factor logic), then computes, for each output cell, the total length of contour line falling within a circular neighborhood -- the Land Surface Ruggedness Index of Beasom, Wiggers, and Giardino (1983), automating the more accurate of the two methods they describe (direct length measurement) rather than their manual dot-grid proxy. Implemented independently of Esri's Line Density tool (which reports a related but different quantity, density rather than total length), using an exact segment/circle-clip length calculation, not a rasterized approximation -- computed as true geodesic ground distance (via 3-D ECEF coordinates on the reference spheroid) on a geographic DEM, so it is correct at any latitude, not just an approximation. The derived contours may optionally be saved. The output is floating point and carries statistics and a histogram; pyramids are built with bilinear resampling.
dataIdInfo.idCredit: Tool by Jeff Jenness, Jenness Enterprises (http://www.jennessent.com). Method: Beasom, S. L., E. P. Wiggers, and J. R. Giardino. 1983. A technique for assessing land surface ruggedness. Journal of Wildlife Management 47:1163-1166. Suggested citation: Jenness, J. (2026). LSRI on DEM. Jenness Enterprises Wildlife Tools for ArcGIS Pro. Available at: http://www.jennessent.com.
